div.head: The Prologue by Baldassare Castiglione
div.p: Today you will be the spectators of a new comedy, called Calandria, written not in verse but in prose; not in Latin but Italian; not ancient but modern. Calandria comes from Calandro, a character whom you will discover to be such a fool that you will find it hard to believe him one of nature’s creations. But if you have seen or heard of similar things (especially concerning Martin of Amelia, who believed the star Diana to be his wife and himself Amen, able at will to become a woman, a god, a fish, or a plant), then it will not seem strange to you that Calandro is so credulous and does so many stupid things. Depicting, as this play does, things commonly said and done, its author has thought it best not to use verse: remember therefore that he is speaking to you in words that are free and natural. That it is not ancient should displease no one of healthy taste, since things that are new are always pleasing and delight an audience more than things which, seen so often, have become flat and stale. The reason it is not in Latin is that the author, desirous of pleasing you to the utmost and wishing for himself as large an audience as possible –since not everyone is a scholar –wished therefore to write it in Italian, so that, understood by everyone, it would be enjoyed by everyone: besides which, the language given us by natural and by God ought not to be less esteemed among us than Latin, Greek, or Hebrew, compared with which ours would not be inferior if we would only exalt, obey, and polish it with the same diligent care as the Greeks and other ancients. That man must be reckoned an enemy who esteems another language over his own. I know well that my own is so dear to me that I would not exchange it for all the other languages now in use: I believe you are of the same sentiment. Therefore you should be pleased to hear the play spoken in your own language –or rather, in our language, not yours, for it is we who do the talking and you who must be quiet. As for those who will claim that the author has stolen certain things from Plautus, we shall say merely that Plautus deserves to be robbed, the snot-nose, for leaving his things to the world without either a key or a watchman. The author swears upon the holy cross, however, that he has not stolen so much as this ( <<snapping his fingers>> ) from Plautus and wishes to be compared with him in his own right. Anyone who doubts this can look up Plautus’ works; he will find that nothing is missing from them. If that is the case, and Plautus has not been robbed, then no one can say that the author is a thief. And if someone should be so stubborn as to insist that he is, we pray that at least he will not curse him openly, threatening him with the Bargello, but that he will go and whisper it secretly into Plautus’ ear. Now here is the man who will recite the argument of the play; prepare to give him your very closest attention by opening wide the cavities of your ears.

div.head: The Argument
div.p: Demetrius, citizen of Modone, had a son named Lidio and a daughter named Santilla. They were twins, so similar in form and appearance that they could not be distinguished excepts for their clothes: this you will not find hard to believe, for, among the many such examples that we could cite, it is sufficient to mention those highborn Roman brothers, Antonio and Valerio Porcari, who were so similar that everybody in Rome mistook the one for the other. As for our own twins, they have been fatherless since they were six: the Turks seized and burned Modone, killing anyone they found in the streets. Their nurse and their manservant, Fannio, in order to save Santilla, dressed her as a boy and called her Lidio; they believed her brother had been massacred by the Turks. Leaving Modone, they were captured and sent as prisoners to Constantinople, where they were rescued by a Florentine merchant named Perillo, who took the three of them to Rome and installed them in his house, where, over the years, they picked up the local language and customs. And now Perillo wants to give his daughter in marriage to Santilla, whom everyone calls Lidio and believes to be a boy. The real Lidio, her brother, escaped alive from Modone with his manservant, Fessenio. Coming to Italy, he settled in Tuscany, where he too learned the language and customs. When he was nearly eighteen, he came to Rome, where he fell in love with, and was loved by, a married woman named Fulvia. In order to accomplish his purpose with her, he frequently visited her in female dress. After many mishaps, Lidio and Santilla finally learn each other’s identity. Take care now, open well your eyes so as not to mistake the one for the other, for I ward you that both are of the same size and general appearance; both are called Lidio; both dress, speak, and laugh alike; both are in Rome today; and presently both of them are going to appear before you. Don’t imagine, however, that they have come here from Rome, so quickly by means of witchcraft: this platform is Rome, which, when it was in its glory, was so large that it contained many cities, towns, and rivers; but now it is so reduced in size that, as you see, it fits comfortably into our own city. And so it is with everything that was once great and powerful.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: How true it is that man makes one plan and fortune makes another for him! Just when we thought we were quietly settled in Bologna, my master Lidio learned that his sister Santilla was alive and in Italy, and immediately his love for her was revived –a love stronger that ever brother felt toward sister, since, being twins, they were so alike appearance, in speech, and in manner that at Modone, if Lidio were dressed as a little girl and Santilla as a little boy, their own mother and nurse could not tell them apart, let alone strangers. God Himself could not have made them more alike, and it was only natural that each should love the other more than himself. Therefore Lidio, who had thought his sister dead, has now set out to find her. Four months ago, coming to Rome to look for her, he met the Roman lady Fulvia and fell in love whit her. So as to have his way with her, he had her husband Calandro hire me as a servant, and with her consent I immediately arranged it so that the lovers could meet whenever they wished by having Lidio visit her dressed as a woman answering to the name of Santilla. But lately, fearful that they should be discovered, he has shown himself increasingly neglectful of her, and pretends that he want to leave Rome. Fulvia is so upset about this that she can scarcely control herself, and has been consulting soothsayers and magicians; she has come to me about it, and has even sent her maid, Samia, who is in her confidence, to Lidio with prayers, with gifts, and with promises to give her son in marriage to his sister, should Lidio succeed in finding her. All of this has been done so openly that if her husband were not more of a sheep than a man he would have known about it long ago –in which case I would have had to take all the blame: it’s a good thing that I know how to take care of myself. I am in an impossible position: it’s bad enough to serve two masters, and I am trying to serve three –the husband, the wife, and my own master. I never have a moment’s rest. Oh, well, I don’t mind too much: a man who has nothing to do is as good as dead, and if it is true that a good servants is never idle, why then I am the best, for I never even have time to clean my ears. And speaking of Lidio, here he comes with Polinico, his teacher. When you see a dolphin, as the saying goes, you know a storm is brewing. I am going to step aside a moment and listen to what they are saying.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: I never would have thought, Lidio, that you would waste your time on idle love affairs. You are becoming an utterly worthless person, and I blame it all on that rascal Fessenio.

p.seg: Aha!

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: You shouldn’t say that, Polinico.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Ah, Lidio, I am wiser than you and that wretched servant of yours.

p.seg: We shall see about that.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: A prudent man always thinks of what may happen in the future.

p.seg: Here we go with the lessons again.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Should this affair of yours become known, you would not only be in danger of your life but would lose the respect of everybody.

p.seg: Stupid pedagogue!

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Nobody has any use for a playboy. And to think that you have been carrying on with one of the most respected women in our city! Take my advice, Lidio, and get out of it before it is too late.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Polinico, I am young, and young people have always been ruled by love; older people can afford to think of more serious things. I must do as love commands, and it has bidden me to love the lady Fulvia even more than I love myself. And I believe that many people, even if they knew, would not hold it against me, for, just as it is a sign of common sense in a woman not to love a man in a higher position, so it is a sign of merit in a man to love a lady of higher birth than himself.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: (approaching) Well said, my master.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: These are arguments that you have learned from that miserable Fessenio.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You are the miserable one.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: (to Fessenio) Actually I’d be surprised if you didn’t try to spoil the good things that people try to do.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I’m not planning to spoil anything of yours.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Nothing is worse than to see the lives of wise men governed by the saying of fools.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I have always given him better advice than you.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: No one can give good advice who has bad habits. If I had known you better, Fessenio, I would not have recommended you so highly to Lidio.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Did I ever ask you for any favors?

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Now I know that when a man praises another he is often deceived; when he criticizes another, he never is.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: The more fool you, for praising someone you did not know well. For my part, I know that when I speak of you I am never wrong.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Have you spoken evil of me?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You have spoken evil of yourself.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: I must be patient. I am not going to argue with you; it would be like shouting at the thunder.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You won’t because you know you are in the wrong.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: I am trying to avoid other means besides words.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: And what harm could you ever do to me in a hundred years?

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Never mind, never mind. You would soon find out.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: My, my! I’d better be careful. Wild beasts can be dangerous.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: I don’t want to argue with a servant.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: That’s enough, Fessenio. Come off it.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: (to Polinico) Don’t threaten me. I may be just a servant, but even a fly has his rages, and even the smallest hair casts its shadow. Do I make myself clear?

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Be quiet, Fessenio.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: (to Fessenio) Let me continue my conversation with Lidio, if you please.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Oh, he’ll do anything for the sake of peace.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: (ignoring Fessenio) Lidio, God has given us two ears so that we can hear well.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: And only one mouth, so as not to talk too much.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: (to Fessenio) I am not speaking to you. (To Lidio) A bad habit is easy to cure when it is new, but not when it has had time to grow old. Get rid of this passion, I tell you.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Ah, me, don’t you know that the companions of love are anger, hatred, enmity, disagreement, ruin, poverty, suspicion, worry, pernicious diseases in the souls of men? Avoid love, avoid it.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Ah, Polinico, I cannot.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: And why?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Damn you anyway, with all your whys and wherefores!

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Everything is subject to the power of love, and there is no sweetness like that of fulfilling one’s desire: without love there is nothing perfect, nothing virtuous, nothing good.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: No one could have said it better.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: There is no greater vice in a servant than flattery. And you, Lidio, do you listen to him? Listen to me instead.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Yes, listen to him; he’s such a pretty piece of merchandise.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Love is like fire, when sulfur or some other vile substance is sprinkled over it, sends off evil odors that suffocate a man.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: And when incense, aloes, and amber are sprinkled over it, it makes a fragrance that will revive even the dead.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Aha, Polinico is caught in his own trap.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Return, Lidio, to what is worthwhile.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What is worthwhile is adjusting to the times.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: What is worthwhile is what is good and honest. I warn you that this affair is going to turn out badly.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: The prophet has spoken!

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Remember that a virtuous soul is not moved by greed.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Nor discouraged by fear.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: (to Fessenio) You also do wrong when you know it is arrogance to ridicule the advice of wise men.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: At the same time that you call yourself a wise man you christen yourself a fool: you know there is no folly like that of attempting the impossible.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: It is better to lose, speaking the truth, than to win telling lies.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I tell the truth as well as you, but I don’t go around criticizing everything and everybody the way you: just because you know a few words of Latin you think everyone except yourself is an idiot. You are not Salomon, you know. You never stop to consider that is right for an old man may not be right for a young one; that what is right in time of danger may not be right at ordinary times. You, who are old, cling to the kind of life that old men remember, but you must allow Lidio, who is young, to lead the kind of life that is proper for young men nowadays, and adjust yourself to the idea.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: It is certainly true that the more servants a man has, the more enemies. This fellow will lead you to the gallows, Lidio, and even if you had no other troubles you would always have a remorseful soul, for there is no torture so great as knowing the mistakes that you have made. Therefore leave this mistress of yours.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: I can no more leave her than a form can leave its shadow.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Indeed, it might be better for you to hate her than to leave her.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Oh, oh! He can’t even carry a calf and you want him to carry an ox.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: She will leave you soon enough.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Oh, all women are not the same.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: They may not look the same but they have the same nature.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: You are wrong there.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Lidio, don’t be blind: they are all alike, and you cannot believe one even when she is dead.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Now I am beginning to see the light.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: What’s that?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You are adjusting to the times.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: I am merely speaking the truth to Lidio. What are you driving at?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I mean that you have made an adjustment to the modern fashion.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: How so?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: In disliking women, as almost everyone at this court does. But when you speak of them in this way, you do them an injustice.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Fessenio is right. I cannot approve of what you have said about women; they are the greatest source of goodness and comfort in the world, and without them we would be useless, inadequate, harsh, and like the beasts of the field.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: It is necessary to say all this? Everyone knows that women are so desirable that nowadays all the men go about imitating them and would willingly become women both in body and in soul.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Such comments do not deserve a reply.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You mean you can’t think of one.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Remember Lidio, that you can still get out of this if you try. For your own good, I beg you once more to do so.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Polinico, there is nothing in the world that heeds advice less than love, whose nature is such that a man will allow himself to be consumed by it rather than give it up because someone tells him to. So that if you try to make me give up this woman it is like trying to catch a shadow or snare the wind in a net.

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: And this worries me very much. You used to be as easily molded as wax, and now you are headed for the worst kind of trouble. You don’t know what this woman is really like, and I warn you once more: This is all going to end very badly for you.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: I don’t believe it, and even if it were true, haven’t you taught me in your lessons that the man who dies in love dies happy?

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Well, I have warned you. Do as you please, and listen to this jackass instead of me: you will soon find out the damage that love can cause.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You have said enough, Polinico. Do you know what damage love causes?

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: What, jackass?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Like a truffle, it causes the fortunes of young men to rise, and old men to fart.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: Polinico
sp.p: Ah, Lidio, you laugh about it, and pay no attention to what I am trying to say. Well, I shall leave you on your own, and go about my business.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What a pity. Did you notice how pious he pretends to be, as if we didn’t know he’s the world’s biggest hypocrite? I haven’t been able to get a word in edgewise, and I have good news about Calandro.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Let us hear it. It may take some of the sting out of Polinico’s words.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Well, now, tell me what has been going on.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Fulvia’s husband, Calandro –that sheep whom I pretend is my master and whom you are cuckolding– seeing you dressed as a woman and calling yourself Santilla, has been completely taken in and has approached me to see if I could arrange for you to sleep with him: I have arranged it for this very evening.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Ho, ho! This is really something. And now that you mention it I remember that the other day, as I was returning from Fulvia dressed as a woman, he followed me for a short distance –I never guessed the reason. Let’s lead him on, shall we?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Leave everything to me. I’ll make him think I’ve done miracles for him, and you may be sure he will believe everything I tell him. I tell him the wildest things in the world and he never once doubts me; he is the world’s biggest simpleton. I could give you a thousand examples, but to make a long story short I will simply say that there is so much nonsense in him that a single speck of it, found in Solomon, Aristotle, or Seneca, would be sufficient to discredit all the wisdom of those men. And the funniest thing of all is that he thinks himself so handsome and so charming that he imagines every woman who sees him falls in love with him, as if he were the most dashing young fellow alive. He is such an ox that it wouldn’t surprise me to see him eat hay, and for this reason it will be easy for us to lead him where we like.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! I am going to die of laughter. But tell me, what’s going to happen when he comes up to me, thinking I am a woman?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I’ll take care of that; leave it to me. But look, I see him now, coming our way. Go quickly: he mustn’t see us together.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Fessenio.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Who’s calling me? Oh, it’s my master.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Tell me, what about Santilla?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You say, what about Santilla?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Well, let’s see... I don’t know for sure, but I think she is wearing a skirt, a blouse, an apron, a pair of gloves, and a pair of slippers.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: You idiot, I don’t want to know what she is wearing, but how she is.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Oh, I see. You want to know how she is.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: If you please.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Well, when I saw her a few minutes ago she was... wait, let’s see... she was sitting with her hand up to her chin, listening while I talked to her about you. Her eyes and mouth were wide open, and her little tongue hung out slightly, like this.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: That’s more like it. So she listened willingly, eh?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Indeed she did. And I have prepared her so that before long you will have your wish.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Good for you, dear Fessenio.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I hope it will be.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Never doubt it. Oh! Fessenio, give me a hand: I am afraid I don’t feel very well.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why, what’s the matter, master? Do you have a fever?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: No, of course not, stupid. It’s Santilla.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Did she hit you?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Oh, what a fool you are! I mean I am so much in love that it hurts.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Well, you will soon be with her.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: What are we waiting for? Let’s go to her now.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Not so fast. There are still a few details I have to attend to.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: All right, but be as quick as you can.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I will; don’t worry.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Don’t forget, now.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: (Exit Calandro.) I won’t. You’ll see. Ha, ha, ha! This is quite a situation: both husband and wife are in love with the same person. And now I see Fulvia’s servant, Samia, coming out of the house. Something is going on; I can tell by the look on her face. I’ll talk to her: she knows everything.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Samia, Samia, wait a minute!

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Oh, hello, Fessenio.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What’s going on inside?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Nothing that’s good for my mistress.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: How do you mean?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: She’s in a bad way.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why, what’s wrong?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: I’d better not say.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Not say what?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Well, frankly, she’s too anxious.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: To do what?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Well... to enjoy herself with Lidio. Do I make myself clear?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Oh, I knew that as well as you.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: But there is something else you don’t know.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: She is sending me to someone who will make Lidio do as she wishes.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Oh? How will this “someone” make him do that?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: By means of songs.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Songs?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: And who is this musician?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Who said anything about a musician? I said she was sending me to someone who would make Lidio go back to her, or die in the attempt.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Who is this fellow?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Ruffo the magician, who will do whatever needs to be done.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: How does he do that?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: He has a linguistic spirit.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You mean a familiar spirit.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: I don’t understand all these words. All I’m supposed to do is tell the magician to come to my mistress. Good-bye, and don’t tell anyone what I’ve said.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Don’t worry; I won’t. Good-bye.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: It’s too early to catch Ruffo at his dinner; I’d better look in the piazza to see if he’s there. Oh, what luck! I see him. Ruffo! Don’t you hear me, Ruffo?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: (turning around) I hear someone calling me.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Ruffo, wait a minute!

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Who can this woman be?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Oh, I am all out of breath.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Well, what is it?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: My mistress begs you to go to her right away.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Who is your mistress?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: The lady Fulvia.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Calandro’s wife?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: What does she want from me?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: She will tell you.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: That’s her house over there, isn’t it?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Yes, it’s only a few steps. Shall we go?

p.seg: Could this be one of the many foolish women who think I am a magician and have a familiar spirit, as they call it? I think I know what she wants, so I’ll go to her house before this fellow who is coming this way gets here.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Now I see that the gods have their jokes as well as human beings: here is love, who is accustomed to dwell in noble hearts, sticking so firmly to this sheep Calandro that it’s impossible to dislodge him. He must not have much to do, to visit such a baboon.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Fessenio, oh, Fessenio!

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Who is it? Oh, it’s you, my master.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Have you seen Santilla?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I have.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: How do things look?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You will have your way, and what a morsel! You certainly have good taste. You must do everything you can to win her.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I’ll get her, even if I have to go nude and barefoot.

p.seg: Just listen to this, all you lovers.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: If I get her, I shall eat her up.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Eat her up! Ah, Calandro, have a little pity. Wild beasts may eat one another, but men don’t eat women. You’re supposed to drink them, no eat them.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Drink them?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Yes, drink them.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: But how?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Don’t you know?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I’m afraid I don’t.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What a pity that a fine-looking fellow like you doesn’t know how to drink women.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Come, tell me how.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: All right. When you kiss one, don’t you suck her lips?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: And when you drink something, don’t you suck it also?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Well, then: when you kiss a woman, you suck her lips, so you are drinking her.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: It does seem so, and yet I have never drunk Fulvia, though I have kissed her many times.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Ah, but that’s because she was kissing you, too. She was sucking your lips at the same time that you were sucking hers, which is why neither of you was drinking the other.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: You are a clever man, Fessenio. It is true that I never once kissed Fulvia without her kissing me in return.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: There, you see?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: But tell me. I used to know a Spanish girl who was always kissing my hand: did that mean she wanted to drink it?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I’ll tell you a secret. When a Spanish girl kissed you, it isn’t because she loves you; it’s because she wants to drink your hands –or rather to suck the rings on your finger.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Fessenio, you know more about women’s secrets!

p.seg: Especially your woman’s.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: That Spanish girl drank two rings of mine. I swear before God that from now on I will never let anybody drink me again.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: A wise decision.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: And I’ll never let anyone kiss me unless I kiss her at the same time.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Yes, do be careful, because if a girl should ever drink your nose, or one of your cheeks, or an eye, you would be the ugliest man in the world.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I’ll be careful, all right. Buy be sure to fix it so I can sleep with Santilla.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Leave it to me. I’ll bring it off.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: And be quiet about it, won’t you?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I am going to see her now, and I’ll be back soon.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: A man should never give up hope: fortune sometimes comes when it is least expected. Fulvia, as I thought, believes I have a familiar spirit. She is passionately in love with a young man, and, every other means having failed, has come to me to see if I can arrange to have him go back to her dressed like a woman. She has promised me money if I can do this, and I think I can because the man she loves is Lidio, a friend of mine from my home town. I also know his servant Fannio, so I shouldn’t have too much trouble. But I haven’t promised her anything; I wanted to talk with Lidio first. The lady Fulvia can make both our fortunes if things go right. I’ll go up to Perillo’s house now, where Lidio is staying. It’s about dinnertime, so he should be there.

div2.head: Scene I
div2.stage: Santilla as Lidio, Fannio, a nurse

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Men are certainly more fortunate than women, and I can bear better witness to this than most women: ever since that day when Modone was burned by the Turks and I dressed as a boy and took my brother’s name, things have gone very well for me. Whereas if I had let it be known that I was a girl, the Turks would have kept me as a slave and not sold me to Perillo, and perhaps Perillo would not have bought me if he had known I was a girl. And now, because he has always been pleased with my behaviour, he wants me to marry his only daughter, whom he plans to leave everything to when he dies. He wants the marriage to take place right away, and therefore I have come to you, nurse, and to you, Fannio, to discuss this thing, which, as you can imagine, causes me some concern.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Shh, quiet! –or this woman I see coming toward us will hear.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: My mistress really has it bad. She says she saw Lidio from her window, so she sent me to talk to him. I’ll see if I can draw him aside. Good day, sir.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Good day.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: May I have a word alone with you, sir?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Who are you?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: You ask me who I am?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Naturally, since I don’t know.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Well, you’ll find out soon enough.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: What is it you want?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: My mistress begs you to love her as she loves you and says you are to feel free to come to her whenever you wish.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I don’t understand. Who is your mistress?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Ah, Lidio, you want to make fun of me.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: It is you who are making fun of me.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: It’s certainly odd that you pretend not to know either me or my mistress. Come, what shall I say to her?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I am not going to answer you until you explain yourself.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: So you don’t understand me, eh?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I don’t understand you; neither do I know you. Nor do I have any desire to. Please be on your way.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: You certainly are discreet. I’ll tell her that much.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Tell her what you like, as long as you leave me alone. I’m tired of looking at you.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: You are, are you? You miserable Greek, you’ll go see my mistress if it cost you your life, because she is sending me to the magician, and his spirit will make you do whatever he wants.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Ah, me, this only proves what I was saying: sad indeed is the fortune of us poor women! Things like this only serve to make me realize it.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: I wish we had got more out of her; it couldn’t have done any harm.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: My mind was on something more important. But is she had been more willing to talk, I would have shown myself more willing to listen.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: I know who she is.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Who?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: The servant of Fulvia, a noble Roman lady.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Oh, I know who you mean. And Fulvia is a good name for her.

div2.head: Scene III
div2.stage: Ruffo, Santilla as Lidio, Tiresia, Fannio

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Hello there!

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Whose voice is that?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: I have been looking everywhere for you.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Hello, Ruffo. What is it?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Good news.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Let’s hear it.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Wait a minute. (To Tiresia) Tiresia, go to the house, see what Perillo is doing about this wedding of mine, and when Fannio comes there, send him back to me so I can find out what’s going on. Today I am going to keep out of sight, “As long as there is time, there is hope”. Go quickly now. (Exit Tiresia) Now, Ruffo, tell me your good news.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Though I have known you and Fannio only a short time, I have grown quite fond of you. After all, we are from the same home town, aren’t we? And now something has come up that can work to our mutual advantage.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: We are fond of you, too, Ruffo, and will be happy to help if we can. But what is it?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: I’ll be brief. Lidio, a certain woman has fallen in love with you and wants you to return her love. Other means having proved unsuccessful, she has come to me; this is because, since I know a few tricks and can read palms, I have the reputation among women –you know how credulous they are –of being a magician. They think I have a familiar spirit by means of which I can do or undo anything I want. I have allowed them to believe this because sometimes it has proved both useful and pleasant –as it will in the case of this woman, if you cooperate. She wants me to persuade you to go to bed with her, and I, thinking you would be agreeable to the idea, have given her some hope. This is all you have to do –it will make us both rich, and you will have the pleasure of sleeping with her as well.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Ruffo, this is a pretty tricky business, and as I have no experience in such things I could easily be made a fool of. I’ll think it over and discuss it with Fannio. But tell me: who is this woman?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Her name is Fulvia. She’s rich, of noble family, and also beautiful.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Oh! The mistress of that woman we were just talking to.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Yes, she’s the one.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Her maid spoke to you?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Just a few minutes ago.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: And what did you say?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I sent her away with strong words.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Too bad. Well, the next time you talk to her you must be more agreeable, if we are to bring this off.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I will.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Tell me, Ruffo, when would Lidio have to go to her?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: The sooner the better.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: By day or by night?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: By day.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Oh, someone would be sure to see me.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: She has thought of that. She wants me to have the spirit make him go in the form of a woman.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: And what good would he be to the lady Fulvia, if your spirit changes him into a woman?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: I think she meant dressed like a woman. Anyway, that’s what she said.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: How very extraordinary! Don’t you think so, Fannio?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: I do indeed. As a matter of fact I like the idea.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Are we agreed, then?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: We’ll let you know in just a moment, after we’ve talked it over.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Where shall we meet?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Right here.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: And whoever comes first will wait for the other.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Good enough. See you soon.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: This makes it easier for you to keep out of sight today, just as you wanted: no one would think of looking for you at Fulvia’s house. And knowing she is a whore, you can buy her silence as often as you please. But what I like best is the humor of the situation. You are a woman, and she wants you to go to her dressed like a woman: thus in satisfying her you will also be disappointing her.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Shall we do it?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: By all means.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Very well. Now go home, find out what’s going on, get me the necessary clothes, and meet me at Franzino’s shop. We’ll tell Ruffo we’ll do as he says.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: You’d better go, too. Here comes someone. Maybe Perillo has sent him to look for you.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: He’s not one of our men. But you’re right; I mustn’t show myself. Good-bye for now.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: There’s the lady Fulvia over there. I’ll go and tell her Lidio is determined to go away, just to see how she takes it.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Welcome, dear Fessenio! Tell me, what news of Lidio?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: He doesn’t seem to be himself today.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Oh? What’s the matter with him?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: He’s taken it into his head to go look for his sister Santilla.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Ah, me. He wants to leave Rome?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: He seems set on it.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Dear Fessenio, if you are interested in your own welfare, or in Lidio’s, and if mine means anything to you, you must urge him, persuade him, beg him not to leave on this account. I will search all Italy for this girl, and if we succeed in finding her, I give you my word that I will give her in marriage to Flaminio, my only son.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Do you want me to promise him this?

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: I have given my word, and I will keep it.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I’m sure he’ll listen willingly to this; it’s a thing that’s certain to please him.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Unless you can help me I am desperate. Plead with him to save my life, for it belongs to him.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I’ll see what I can do. For your sake.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: For yours, too, dear Fessenio! Remember that.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Well, well, may God have pity on her. It’s a good thing that Lidio is planning to pay her a visit today, dressed like a woman as he always does at such times. Though she doesn’t know it, he’s as hot for it as she is. But first I have to attend to Calandro, and there he is now. I’ll tell him everything is ready.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Greetings, master! You are in luck, for I bring good news. Give me your hand.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: My hand –and my foot.

p.seg: My, how witty we are today!

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: (grumpily) What’s this news of yours that’s supposed to be so good?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What is it? Why, man, the world is your oyster.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I mean that Santilla loves you even more than you love her, because I told her how generous you are, how good looking, and how wise. And now she is as eager for the bed as you are. I no sooner mentioned your name than she got all excited: you’re going to be the happiest man in all the world.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Are you telling me the truth? Ah, I can’t wait to suck those red lips and lovely cheeks, the color of wine and cottage cheese.

p.seg: Blood and milk –his favorite diet.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Dear Fessenio, you shall name your own reward.

p.seg: Such kindness, all of a sudden!

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Let’s go to her now.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Oh, no, you can’t do that! Do you think she’s a common whore? You will have to do this thing properly.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Well then, how am I to go to her?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: On your feet.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I know that, but in what manner?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: If you went there openly, someone would be sure to see you, so we have decided that you must hide in a trunk and let yourself be carried into her room: in that way you can best fulfill your mutual desire.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Ah, so I don’t go on my feet after all.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I can see you are a shrewd one. That’s right.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: It won’t be too uncomfortable, will it, Fessenio?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Will the trunk be big enough that I can get all of me inside?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What difference does that make? If we can’t get you inside in one piece, we can do it in little pieces.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Little pieces? How do you mean?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Just so. Little pieces.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: But how?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why, don’t you know?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I do not.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: If you had ever sailed on a ship, you would. Because when there are hundreds of people that have to be fitted into a boat, the only way it can be done is to take a leg from one, an arm from another, and so on until they are all netly stowed away like any other kind of cargo. That way they don’t take up so much room.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: But what happens after that?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why, when they get into port, each person claims the part of him that has been taken away, and sometimes, whether through carelessness or malice, a man will take a limb that belongs to someone else: that’s bad, because it’s either too big or too small, which makes him look crippled and lopsided. Now do you understand?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I do, and I shall take care that my member is not exchanged for someone else’s.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: If you don’t exchange it yourself, no one else is going to: that’s for certain. Anyway, you’ll be all alone in there. Of course you may have to be divided up before we can fit you in.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Where are the best places to divide a man?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why, wherever you see a bulge or a prominence of some kind, like up here, or down here. Would you like to see how it’s done?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: If you please.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: There’s nothing to it, just a bit of magic. You have to repeat what I say, but in a low voice, because if you should shout, everything would be spoiled.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: First we’ll start with your hand. Give it to me, and repeat after me: Ambracullac.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Anculabrac.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: (tugging his arm) You said it wrong. Try again: Ambracullac.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Alabrucuc.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: (again tugging his arm) That’s even worse. Ambracullac.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Alucumbrac.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: No, no, no! look, say: Am.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Am.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Bra.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Bra.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Cul.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Cul.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Lac.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Lac.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Stupid.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Stupid.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Ox.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Ox.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Now.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Now.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You’re.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Yo’re.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Going.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Going.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: To.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: To.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: (Twisting his arm violently.) Get it!

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Ouch! Oh, my poor arm.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Didn’t I tell you not to raise your voice? I never saw anyone with such a short memory and so little patience. Now you have broken the spell.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: And you have broken my arm.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: It’s no use. We won’t be able to divide you up.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: How shall we manage, then?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I’ll have to find a truck big enough to hold you as you are.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I hope you can, because I don’t like all this dividing. My arm is killing me.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I’ll go look for one now.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: And I’ll go to the marketplace and come right back.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Now I must find Lidio and tell him about this: it’s so funny we’ll be supplied with laughs the rest of the year. I’m going now because I don’t want to have to talk with Samia, whom I see over there muttering to herself.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Ah, me, such is life! It hasn’t been more than a month since Lidio wanted to spend every minute with my mistress, and now, when he sees how much she is in love with him, he pays her no attention. If we don’t find some way out of this, I don’t know what Fulvia will do; she might cause a scandal, and I have a feeling that Calandro’s brother already suspect something . Heaven knows it’s obvious enough: all she thinks about is Lidio. How true it is that he who has love in his heart has spurs in his side!

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Samia!

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Coming!

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Tiresia told you this?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: They are taking the wedding for granted?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: They are.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Does Virginia seem happy about it?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: She can hardly wait.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: They are getting everything ready, then?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Yes, indeed; they have turned the house upside down.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: They think I am pleased?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Evidently.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Ah, me! What causes others to be happy causes me nothing but pain. The affection that Perillo and his wife have for me hurts like a sharp arrow: I can’t do what they want, but neither can I do what would be best for myself. Oh, if God had only given me death instead of life, and a grave instead of a cradle when I came out of my mother’s womb, then this situation would never have arisen: my fortune would have ended where it began. Oh, my poor brother, you who met with such an untimely death in our fatherland (or so at least I believe), if only you were here to advise me! What is poor Santilla going to do now –since henceforth I must call myself Santilla and not Lidio? I am a woman, yet I must also be a bridegroom! If I marry Virginia, they will find out I am a woman and not a man: they will turn me out and might even have me put to death. And if I refuse to marry her, they will also turn me out, with their curses. If I reveal myself now to be a woman, I would only bring harm upon myself. I can’t stand much more of this, though. A cliff on one side, wolves on the other!

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Don’t give up hope; something may yet turn up. I think you are right to keep out of Perillo’s sight, and this idea of Ruffo’s for you to go to Fulvia in women’s clothes is a good one. I have them all ready for you. We must do one thing at a time, as they come.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I wonder what is keeping Ruffo.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Remember what we said: whoever came first was to wait for the others.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: We’d better not stay here, or that fellow over there might see us. He may have been sent by Perillo, though I doubt it.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Things couldn’t possibly work out better. Lidio is dressing up as a woman, and Calandro is waiting for him in a room on the first floor of his house. Lidio, looking simply irresistible, will visit him there, and then when the old fool’s back is turned, we’ll slip in a Prostitute through the back door to take his place. He’s such a fool that he can’t tell a nightingale from a jackass, and will never know the difference. Here he comes now; see how happy he looks. God bless you, master.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: And you, too, dear Fessenio. Is the trunk ready?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Yes, and it’s so big you won’t even get your hair mussed.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: That’s fine. But tell me something.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Yes?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Should I stay awake in the trunk, or go to sleep?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What do you mean, awake or asleep? Don’t you know that when you are on a horse you ride, when you are in the streets you walk, when at table you eat, when in bed you sleep, and when you are in a trunk you die?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Die? What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Just that. Die, Why?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Damn! That’s not so good.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Didn’t you ever die before?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Not that I know of.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Then if you’ve never been dead, how do you know it’s so bad?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Did you ever die?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Oh, yes! Thousands of times.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Does it hurt?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: No more than sleeping.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Do I absolutely have to die?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Absolutely, when you get in the trunk.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: But who will kill me?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You will have to do it yourself.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: And how do I go about it?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: There’s nothing to it. But since you don’t know, I’ll tell you.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: If you please.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You close your eyes, clench your hands together, twist your arms, and then keep very still and very quiet. Finally you neither see nor hear anything.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I see. But how do I come back to life?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: That’s one of the greatest secrets in the whole world; hardly anybody knows it. I wouldn’t tell it to anyone but you, and you must swear not to repeat it to a single soul.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I swear I won’t tell it to anybody, not even to myself.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Oh, it’s all right to tell it to yourself –but only to one ear, not to both.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Promised. Now tell it to me.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Well, Calandro, you know that the only difference between the dead and the living is that the living move around and the dead do not. And if you do exactly as I say, you will come back to life all right.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Tell me how.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: First you must raise your head and spit straight up in the air, then you give your whole body a shake. Next you open your eyes, say a few words, and move your arms and legs. That always chases death away, and you may be sure, Calandro, that whoever is able to do this is never dead. Now you are in possession of one of the world’s greatest secrets.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I appreciate your confidence. Now I die and come back to life whenever I like.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: That you can, master.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: And I’ll be careful to do it exactly right.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I’m sure you will.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Shall I try it once, just to make sure?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: A good idea. Are you ready?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Make an ugly face. Uglier still. There! A fine corpse if ever I saw one. There’s nothing like a little know-how. Who would ever have thought this man would learn to die so well? At least he looks dead on the outside: if he’s as dead on the inside as he is on the outside, it’s a perfect job. We’ll see. (Makes magical motions) Calandro! Oh, Calandro!

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: (weakly) I’m dead. I am dead.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Come back to life, Calandro. Spit in the air.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: (sighing) Ah, ah. You should have let me alone.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I was just beginning to see the next world.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You’ll have plenty of time to see it in the trunk.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I can hardly wait.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: That’s the right spirit. Now that you know how to die and come back to life so well, we mustn’t waste time.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: That’s right. Are we ready?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Not quite. We have to make sure that your wife doesn’t suspect anything. You tell her you are going to the country, and go instead to Menicuccio’s house. I’ll have everything ready and meet you there.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: All right. I’ll do it now, since the beast is ready.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: (Inspects Calandro’s lower parts) It’s ready, is it? Let’s have a look.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Ha, ha! I mean my mule is ready.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I knew what you meant; I was only joking.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: It’s been a long time since I was in the saddle, but I’d do anything for that little angel that’s waiting for me up there.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Angle, eh? Today we’re going to see stupidity joined to filth. He’s gone now to mount his mule, and I’ll go tell that pretty little Prostitute to get everything ready and wait for me. There is Calandro, already in the saddle. What a lot of strength there must be in that little mule to carry such a stupid old elephant!

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Fulvia.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: What is it?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Come to the window.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: What do you want?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I’m going to the farm, to see Flaminio.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: When are you coming back?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Maybe tonight sometime.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: All right. Good-bye. (Exit Calandro) And bad luck! A fine husband my brothers married me off to! I can’t stand the sight of him.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Ladies and gentlemen, we have here the spoils of love: whoever wants to acquire politeness, insight, and knowledge need only buy these clothes and wear them awhile. They belong to Calandro, who took them off when he got into the trunk –a man so clever that he has fallen in love with another man, believing him a woman, and so powerful that he can die and come back to life as he chooses. Let whoever wants to buy them show the color of his money: I can sell them with a clear conscience as they belong to a dead man. Ha, ha! And now Lidio, dressed as a woman, is waiting merrily for this handsome lover, who, to tell truth, is uglier than Bramante himself. I ran ahead to meet the Prostitute that I made an appointment with; she is going to cooperate. Here she is now, and there is the porter with the trunk, which he believes is full of precious merchandise: he doesn’t know that it contains the vilest stuff on earth. Doesn’t anybody want these clothes? No? Well, good-bye then. Be of good cheer: I am going to lead the gelding to the mare.

div2.head: Scene II
div2.stage: A Prostitute, Fessenio, a porter, two or three customs inspectors, Calandro

sp.speaker: Prostitute
sp.p: Here I am, Fessenio. Let’s go.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Let the trunk go first. No, porter, not that way. Over here.

sp.speaker: Prostitute
sp.p: What’s inside?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Something for you, pettikins.

sp.speaker: Prostitute
sp.p: What is it?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Silks and fine clothes.

sp.speaker: Prostitute
sp.p: Whose are they?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: They belong to the man you are going to entertain, my dear.

sp.speaker: Prostitute
sp.p: Oh, will he give some of them to me?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Yes, if you do what I said.

sp.speaker: Prostitute
sp.p: I will. Don’t you worry.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Remember that your name is Santilla, and everything else I told you.

sp.speaker: Prostitute
sp.p: Leave everything to me.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Otherwise you won’t get a penny.

sp.speaker: Prostitute
sp.p: I say don’t worry. What do these customs inspectors want with the porter?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Quiet! And listen.

sp.speaker: Prostitute
sp.p: Tell me, what’s inside that trunk?

sp.speaker: Porter
sp.p: Why, what’s the matter?

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: Have you passed the customs?

sp.speaker: Porter
sp.p: No, sir.

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: What’s inside?

sp.speaker: Porter
sp.p: I don’t know.

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: Better tell the truth.

sp.speaker: Porter
sp.p: They told me it was silk. Dresses and such as that.

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: Silk?

sp.speaker: Porter
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: Is it locked?

sp.speaker: Porter
sp.p: I don’t think so.

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: Set in down.

sp.speaker: Porter
sp.p: Ah no, sir.

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: Set in down, stupid. Do you want me to hit you?

sp.speaker: Porter
sp.p: Oh, oh! Our plan is spoiled. He is going to find out everything, and we shall all be ruined.

sp.speaker: Prostitute
sp.p: What’s the matter?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Our plain is spoiled. (To Prostitute) Sofilla, you must help me.

sp.speaker: Prostitute
sp.p: What can I do?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Cry, shout, tear your hair, as if you were mourning for someone.

sp.speaker: Prostitute
sp.p: But why?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You will soon find out.

sp.speaker: Prostitute
sp.p: (weeping loudly) Boohoo! Boohoo!

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: What’s this? Somebody dead?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: (approaching, to Inspector) What are you looking for?

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: The porter told us this trunk contained dutiable merchandise, instead of which it seems to contain a corpse.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: That’s right, It does.

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: Who is it?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: It’s this poor woman’s husband. Don’t you see how hard she is taking it?

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: Why are you carrying him in a trunk?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: To fool the police, if you must know.

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: To fool the police? Why?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Because no one would have anything to do with us if they found out the truth.

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: What is the truth?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: This man in dead of the plague.

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: The plague! Oh, and I touched it!

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: To your harm, I fear.

sp.speaker: Inspector
sp.p: Where are you taking him?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Someplace we can bury him, or drop him in the river.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: (sitting up in trunk) You want to drown me, do you? But I’m not dead, you rascals. I’m not dead, I say!

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Oh, everyone is running away, and no wonder: this is the work of the devil. Run, Sofilla! Run, porter! Run, everybody!

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: (emerging from trunk, striking Fessenio) So you wanted to drown me, did you, you wretch?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why, master, what’s the matter? Why do you want to hit me?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: You want to know why, do you?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Because you deserve it, you scoundrel. That’s why.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: This is what comes of trying to do a good deed. Are you angry with me because I have saved your life?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: And how did you save mi life, may I ask?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why, I kept you from going to the customhouse, didn’t I?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: And suppose I had gone there, what would have happened?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What would have happened? I should have let them carry you there –then you’d have seen.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: What the devil do you mean?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You act as if you were born yesterday. You were being smuggled: they would have sold you just as they do everything that’s smuggled.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Well, then, you did right after all. Forgive me, Fessenio.

p.seg: I’ll get even with him for this.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I will. But tell me, who was that ugly-looking woman who ran away just now?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Ah, don’t you know her?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: That was death, who was with you in the trunk.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: With me? What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Just that. With you.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I didn’t see her there.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You don’t see sleep either, do you, when you are sleeping? Or thirst when you drink, or hunger when you eat? You don’t see life either, for that matter, although you are alive. But it is with you just the same.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: It’s true I have never seen these things.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Exactly. And when you die, you don’t see death.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: H’m. Why did the porter run away?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: He was afraid of death. So I’m afraid you won’t be able to see Santilla today.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Then I might as well be dead.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I don’t know how I can arrange it now –unless you are willing to do a little work.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Fessenio, I’ll do anything to see her. I’ll even go to bed barefoot.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Oh, no, nothing like that.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: What, then?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You’ll have to be the porter yourself. Nobody will be able to tell the difference: you’ve already taken for a short time, your face has changed somewhat, too. I’ll pretend I’m the carpenter who made the trunk. Don’t worry about Santilla. She’ll put two and two together immediately: she’s a regular sibyl.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: A good idea. I would do anything to gain Santilla’s love.

p.seg: Did you ever see such an anxious lover?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: (groaning) Fine.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Well then, carry it to her house. I’ll follow and meet you at the door. (Exit Calandro.) That jackass’s load is becoming to him. Now I have to find the Prostitute and lead her into the house by the back door. I’m afraid Lidio may have to let Calandro kiss him, but no matter –Fulvia’s kisses will then seem all the sweeter. Here comes Samia. She didn’t see Calandro talking with me –fortunatley.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Where have you been?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: To Ruffo the magician. My mistress sent me.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What did he say?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: That he was coming to see her.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: My, my, women are so silly. Well, I have to go find Lidio and tell him what your mistress asked me to.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Is he at home?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: What do you think he will do?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Frankly, I’m not too hopeful. But I can’t say for sure.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Things certainly don’t seem to be turning out very well for my mistress and me. Well, good-bye.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Good-bye.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: My mistress is not going to like this. Neither Lidio nor Ruffo’s familiar spirit has given her much encouragement.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Why were you gone so long?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: I wasn’t able to find Ruffo until just now.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: What does he say?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: That the spirit answered him... how was it? I don’t remember.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: You goose-brain, you’d better remember!

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Oh, yes, now it is coming back to me. He said he made an ambiguous reply.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: You mean ambiguous?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Yes, that’s it. Ambiguous.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: He said nothing else?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: That he was going to try again.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: That he was at your service and that as soon as he had anything good to report, he would come here right away.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Ah, me! That’s not so good. But what about Lidio?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: He thinks about as much of you as he would a pair of old shoes.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Did you find him?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Yes, and talked with him, too.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Well, what did he say?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: You won’t like it.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Ah, me! Tell me anyway.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: He pretends he never met you.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: What are you saying?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: That’s the way it is.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: How could you have understood him to say such a thing?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: He spoke to me in a way that frightened me.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Maybe he was joking with you.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: No, my lady. He was insulting.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Maybe you didn’t talk to him right.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Bo, my lady. You should never have sent me.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Maybe someone was with him, eh?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: I took him aside.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Maybe you talked too loud.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: I whispered into his ear.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: But what did he say?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: He drove me away.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: He doesn’t love me anymore, then. Is that it?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: No, nor respect you either.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: You really think so?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: I know it.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Alas, can I believe my own ears?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: You can, my lady.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: He didn’t ask you how I was.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: He said he never heard of you.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: So he’s forgotten me, has he?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: You’re lucky that he doesn’t hate you.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: How unhappy I am! I know now for certain that Lidio is unfaithful. How sad is the destiny of women! And how few women find lovers who are completely satisfactory! Poor me, I loved too deeply and gave so much of myself that I am no longer my own mistress! Cruel heavens, why don’t you make Lidio love me as I love him, or let me run away from him as he runs away from me? But what am I thinking of? –Not to love Lidio, and to run away from him? Ah, no, I can’t do that, nor do I want to. On the contrary, I am going to seek him out. Why, since he has come to me so often in women’s clothes, shouldn’t I, just this once, try going to him dressed like a man? It’s reasonable enough, and he might even appreciate my going to such trouble on his account. Why don’t I do it then? I there any reason why I should pine away like this? There is no pain like that of a woman who has wasted her youth, and whoever thinks that once it’s gone you can get it back is mistaken. When will I ever find another Lidio? A man like that is worth any amount of trouble. And now is the right time, because he’s at home and my husband is away at the farm. Who dares to stop me then? My mind is made up; I shall do it. I didn’t think that magician was going to do much good anyway. The best way to get something done is to do it yourself. Others do it at their own convenience and never take the same interest. If I go to him myself, he will see my tears, hear my sobs, and listen to my prayers: I shall throw myself at his feet, hug him around the neck, and pretend to die. No one could be so cruel as not to take pity on me then. No one hearing words of love spoken straight from the heart could possibly be indifferent to them, and in love all things are possible. Therefore I am going to dress myself up like a man and go to him. Samia, you stay here at the door and don’t let anyone linger in front of the house: if somebody sees me coming out, they might recognize me.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: How unhappy we poor women are! When we fall in love, we are done for. Fulvia, who was always so prudent, doesn’t know what she’s doing now that she’s in love with Lidio. Since hw won’t come to her, she has decided to go to him dressed like a man, never thinking of what might happen if she were discovered. Well, she ought to be satisfied now: she’s given him everything, including her honour and her body, and he thinks no more of her than of the dirt under his feet. Our sex is truly to be pitied. Here she is already, rigged out in men’s clothes. It didn’t take her long.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Well, Samia, I am of to find Lidio. You stay here and keep the door locked until I come back. Do you understand?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Yes, my lady. But do be careful.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Love can make a person do anything. I used to be so timid I was afraid to leave my room alone, and now, moved by love, I don’t even hesitate to leave the house alone in men’s clothing. I am going straight to Lidio’s house, though it’s a good distance, and I’ll make him listen to me. No one will be there except the old woman who waits on him and maybe Fessenio, who knows everything anyway. No one will recognize me; I don’t have anything to worry about. And even be sorry than not to act and be sorry; nothing ventured, nothing gained.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: She is gone to seek her pleasure. I was wrong to blame her, for he who is indifferent to love is no better than a beast of the field. I am never so happy myself as when I am with my lover Lusco, who is waiting for me now in the courtyard. We’ll have the whole house to ourselves. I’ll follow my mistress’ example: a person’s a fool not to take his pleasure when the opportunity comes along. (Calling.) Lusco! Oh, Lusco!

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Calandro is with the Prostitute now; they’ll have some pretty secrets between them. I must tell Fulvia what’s going on –she will die laughing. And no wonder! It’s enough to make a dead man laugh. (Approaches Calandro’s house, knocks.) H’m. The door seems to be locked. Hello there! Anybody home?

div2.head: Scene X
div2.stage: Fessenio outside Calandro’s house, Samia inside

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: (knocking) Anybody there? Can’t you hear me? Open up!

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Who’s knocking?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: It’s me, Fessenio. Let me come in, Samia.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Wait a minute.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What’s the matter? Why don’t you open the door?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: I’m trying to put the key in the lock.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Haven’t you got in yet?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: I’m trying. Oh, it’s no use. I can’t do it.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why not?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: The hole is stopped up.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Blow on the key.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: I’m doing the best I can.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why are you taking so long?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: I have it nice and wer now; it ought to do the trick.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Well, hurry up.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: There, you hear? It’s unlocked now; you can come in.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why do you have everything locked up like this?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: My mistress’ orders. She wanted the door locked.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: With you I can talk freely. She has gone to Lidio dressed like a man.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Samia! You don’t mean it?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: I do indeed. I’m supposed to stay here and keep everything locked up until she comes back.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Truly there is nothing too dangerous or too foolish for a lover to attempt: here Fulvia has gone to Lidio’s house, not knowing that her husband is also there. He is bound to believe the worst, seeing her there alone and dressed like a man. He’ll be so furious he may notify her relatives. I’d better hurry to see if there is something I can do. Oh, heavens, here comes Fulvia now, and she has Calandro with her, leading him by the collar. I’ll step aside and listen; that away I’ll find out what has happened.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: So you were going to the farm, were you? You miserable creature, don’t you have enough to do at home that you go prowling around like this? And to think that this is the man I have given my love to and remained faithful to all these years! Now I know why you have been keeping away from me the last few night: you’ve been saving your energy. I don’t know how I keep myself from tearing your eyes out. Did you think you could pull the wool over my eyes so easily? I heard about it before this, and that’s why I dressed myself up like this –to find out for myself if it was true. And now I’m leading you by the collar, like the dirty dog you are, so that all the world can see and take pity on me who have had to put up with your outrages. Do you suppose that if I were like you, and didn’t care what I did, I couldn’t have a good time, too? I’m not as old or as ugly as all that. And it’s only because I have some self-respect that I didn’t revenge myself on that woman I found you with. But I’m not finished yet: I’m going to get even with you both.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Have you finished?

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Than, damn you, I’m the one who ought to be angry. I was enjoying a paradise on earth when you came along and spoiled everything. You are not worth one of her old shoes, for at least she knows how to make love. Her lips are sweeter than wine, she shines brighter than Diana, and she has the wisdom of a Fata Morgana. And if you do her harm, you had better watch out.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: That’s enough out of you. Inside the house! Inside, I say!

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Well, well, live and learn. O love, how great is your power! What poet, what doctor, what philosopher can hope to rival you as teacher? All knowledge, all doctrine is secondary to yours. What else but love would have enabled Fulvia, in so tight a spot, to act so intelligently? I never saw anything like it. There she is over there, standing in her doorway. I’ll say something encouraging to her about Lidio –that’ll cheer her up. Poor thing! I feel sorry for her.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Ah, Fessenio, see how unlucky I’ve been –to find instead of Lidio, that wretched husband of mine. But I got out of it all right.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I know; I heard everything. Don’t show yourself too plainly –somebody might see you in those clothes. There, that’s better.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: You are right. I don’t seem to be able to think about anything but Lidio. Tell me, dear Fessenio, have you seen him?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Yes, my lady.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Recently?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I have, my lady.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: What does he say?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: He’s not going to leave Rome right away.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: But when will I be able to speak with him?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Maybe today. I was on my way to talk with him when I saw you and Calandro.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Try once more, dear Fessenio. For us both.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I’ll see what I can do. Meanwhile try not to worry.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Try not to worry, eh? That’s a good one. I won’t have a moment’s peace till you get back.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Good-bye, my lady.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Good-bye, Fessenio, and don’t be long. (Exit Fessenio.) This suspense is killing me. Samia, tell me what I ought to do.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Maybe Ruffo’s spirit will be able to think of something.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: He’s certainly takin his time about it. Samia, go and see the magician again.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Very well, my lady.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Remind him that we are waiting, and come back at once.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Just as soon as I find him, my lady.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Oh, what luck! There is Ruffo. God bless you, sir.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Hello, Samia, What is it?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: My mistress is dying to know if you have any news for her.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: I believe everything is going to be all right.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: But when?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: I am going to make a complete report to Fulvia.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: All this is taking so long.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Samia, there are some things that can’t be rushed. The stars have to be just right, and I have to find the right magical words; then I have to gather herbs, rocks, and water from various wells. Finally I have to summon my familiar spirit. All these things naturally take time.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Weel, as long as it works in the long run.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: There is every reason for hope.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: (looking offstage) Oh, oh! Do you know who her lover is?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Not for sure.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: (pointing to Santilla as Lidio, who has just appeared) It’s that man over there.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Do you know him well?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: I should think so. Less than two hours ago I was talking with him.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: What did he have to say?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: He acted as if I were some sort of criminal.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Go try again: see if the spirit hasn’t softened him up a bit.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Shall I?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: By all means.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Well, I’ll try.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: After you talk with him, go back to Fulvia and tell her I’m coming to see her right away.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Yes, sir.

p.seg: I’ll step aside and listen to this conversation.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Oh, Lidio, here is Fulvia’s maid coming toward us. Remember that her name is Samia, and be nice to her.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I intend to.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Well, sir, are you still upset?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: No, no, not at all. Samia, I hope you’ll forgive me. The last time I saw you I had something on my mind; I wasn’t my usual self. How is my beloved Fulvia?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Do you really want to know?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Indeed I do.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: She wants you to give her your heart.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I can’t do that.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Why not?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Don’t you know that it already belongs to her?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: God only knows if you are telling the truth. First you couldn’t even remember her, and now you want me to believe that she is your only love –as if I didn’t know that you don’t love her and don’t want to go near her.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: On the contrary, until I see her again I am as good as dead.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: The spirit certainly seems to have done a good job. So you will go to see her as usual?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: As usual? How do you mean?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Why, dressed as a woman.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Ah, yes, of course. Dressed like a woman. Yes, of course. Tell her that.

sp.speaker: Samia
