sp.p: Oh, sir, that will make her so happy! I’d better not linger here any longer, and I’ll take the back street home. It wouldn’t do for anybody to see me talking to you and then going back to lady Fulvia. Good-bye, sir.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Good-bye.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Did you hear that?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Yes, and I heard that “as usual”, too. It’s obvious she’s mistaking you for someone else.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: It seems so.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: We’d better tell Ruffo about this. Here he is now.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Well, gentlemen, have you made up your minds?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: You don’t think we’d let something like that slip through our fingers, do you?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Aha, our friend has reconsidered. Well, you are right, Ruffo, because she’s a great beauty.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I know all about her.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: (to Santilla) You are sure to again some pleasure from it.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: And profit as welll.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Ruffo, if I understand you correctly, you said that Fulvia came to you, other means having failed, from which I gather that she has tried other means. From something that happened today, we have reason to believe that Lidio has been mistaken by her –and by her maid as well –for someone else. Therefore it will be necessary, as a precaution, for you to tell her to make no reference to what has happened in the past. Otherwise she would find out everything, and there would be a terrible scandal. Be sure to warn her of this.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: You were wise to think of this precaution, and I’ll not forget to do as you say. Well, we’re wasting time here; let’s get this thing started. I’d better go to her first.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: We’ll meet you here when you come back.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Lidio, you go ahead. I’ll be along in a minute. (Exit Santilla.) Ruffo, let me have a word with you.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: I’am going to tell you a secret. You’d never guess it, no matter how hard you tried. But you must promise not to tell it to a single soul.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: May God deny my every wish, if I ever breathe a word of it.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: If you do, I will be ruined, and you would not gain the reward you expect.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Don’t worry. What is it?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: My master, Lidio, is a hermaphrodite.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: A hermaphrodite. Well, what of it?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Not hermaphrodite. Hermaphrodite. Heavens, how dense you are!

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: What does that mean?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Don’t you know?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: No; that’s why I ask.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: A hermaphrodite is someone who is half man and half woman.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Is Lidio like that?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: He is.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: You mean he has the sex organs of a woman and the sex organs of a man, too?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Come to think of it, I always thought there was something a little effeminate in his voice and manner.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: This first time, therefore, he will use only the woman’s organs with Fulvia. She will think that this is because she asked him to come in the form of a woman; she’ll think the spirit did this to please her, and she’ll have so much faith in his power that she will worship you forever, for being his master.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: This is one of the best schemes I have ever heard: we stand to make a fortune.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Is the woman generous?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: I should think so! True lovers, you know, share everything they have –money, clothes, livestock, everything. A woman who loves as deeply as the lady Fulvia would even give her life.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: What you say please me.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: As what you have told me about that hermaphrodite please me.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: I’m glad you can’t pronounce that word, because even if you wanted to repeat it you couldn’t.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Better go to Lidio’s now and get yourselves dressed up. I’ll tell Fulvia she can expect him.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: I’m to go as my master’s maid. Right?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Right. And be sure to be ready when I come back.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: I will. It’s a good thing I have the necessary clothes.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: So far things couldn’t have worked out better. By now Samia has probably spoken with Fulvia, and she’ll be waiting for me. I’ll tell her the spirit has arranged everything; then I’ll give her this image and tell her to say certain words and make certain gestures before it, that this will bring about what she wants, and I shall warn her not to say a word about it to anyone except her maid. Ah, I see Samia now, standing in the doorway.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Come in, Ruffo. My mistress is waiting for you downstairs, because her sheep of a husband is upstairs.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: What is it, Fessenio?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I have to see the lady Fulvia.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: She can’t see you now.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why not?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: She’s with the magician.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Let me in anyway.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: No, I can’t.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Women are such fools.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Maybe yours are.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: It’s a good thing I know how to hold my temper. I’ll take a walk and come back later.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: That’s a good idea.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: If Fulvia knew what I knew, she wouldn’t worry about spirits. Lidio yearns for her even more than she does for him; he wants to see her this very day. But I want to be the one to tell her this, because I know she’ll give me something. I’m not going to let Samia do it; that’s why I didn’t tell her anything. But I must go now: if Fulvia were to see me, she might think I came to see her magician, who must be that man I see coming out of the house.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Everything is going beautifully. Fulvia has given me a nice sum of money; at this rate my fortune will soon be made, and then good-bye to these rags. What a stroke of luck! This is a rich woman and, unless I am badly mistaken, more in love than she is wise. She’ll have need of me again, unless I miss my guess. Isn’t it strange how people’s dreams sometimes come true? Last night I dreamed I caught a pheasant. I pulled the pretty feathers from his tail and stuck them in my cap. If the lady Fulvia lets herself be caught like this, as I think she will, I’ll pluck her likewise. Then I’ll be well off for a while, at least, and I’ll know how to make the most of that. But who is that woman I see waving to me? I don’t know her.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Fannio! Your disguise is so good I didn’t recognize you.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Am I pretty?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Yes, indeed. And now go and console the lady Fulvia.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: I’m afraid she won’t get much consolation –not this time, anyway.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Why, yes she will. Lidio is going to use the female organ with her.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: That’s right. Well, shall we go?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Yes. Is Lidio ready?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: He’s waiting for me nearby, and he’s done such a good job that no one would ever guess he wasn’t a woman.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Wonderful. Well, Fulvia is expecting you, so get Lidio and go to her. I’ll wait here and see what happens. I see she is standing on her doorstep now, waiting. It didn’t take her long to get ready.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: No need to worry anymore, my lady.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I mean that Lidio is more anxious to see you than you are to see him. No sooner did I tell him what you asked me to than he got himself ready; he’s on his way here now.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Dear Fessenio, this is the kind of news I like to hear, and you shall be rewarded for it. Listen to Calandro upstairs, asking for his clothes so he can go out again. Better not stay, or he’ll see us together. Oh, how glad you have made me! Things are really looking up now. As soon as I have let that buzzard out of his cage, I shall feel free.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: These lovers are going to make up for lost time, and if Lidio is wise, he’ll forget about his sister. Calandro won’t be at home; they will have lots of time to enjoy themselves. I can afford to take a walk now. Ah, Calandro is coming out. I’d better go, because if he stop to talk with me, he might see Lidio, who ought to be here any minute.

div2.head: Scene XXIII
div2.stage: Calandro, Lidio as Santilla, Santilla in woman’s dress accompanied by Fannio in woman’s dress

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: I see I am in luck: no sooner do I step outside the house than I see my beloved coming my way. Heavens! What shall I say to her? Good morning? No, it’s not that early. Good evening? No, it’s not that late. Good bless you? No, too casual. Mistress of my soul? But that’s not a greeting. Heart of my body? No, too commonplace. Angel face? Too vulgar. Divine spirit? No, that’s not right either. Oh, my, here she is now. Spirit, heart, angel: which shall I say? Oh, damn, what a fool I am! I was mistaken; this isn’t Santilla –there she is over there. (Addresses Santilla.) Good morning... that is, good evening. Oh, no, she’s not the one. It must be the other one after all. (Approaches Lidio.) No, I think it was the other. No, it must be this one. No, it’s the other. Damn!

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: This madman thinks I am a woman: he has fallen in love with me and will follow me all the way to his house. I’ll go home, change, and go to Fulvia later.

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: It’s the one across the street. I’ll go follow her.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: (Follows Lidio)(to Fannio) He’s gone the other way. Quick, now –let’s slip inside before he comes back. There is Fulvia, waiting to let us in.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Samia, oh, Samia!

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Yes, my lady.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Come down here right away!

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Coming.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Faster, for God’s sake. Faster!

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Here I am. What is it?

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Go quickly, find Ruffo the magician, and tell him to come here at once.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Let me go upstairs and get my hat.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Forget your hat, stupid! Go as you are. There’s not a moment to lose!

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: (grumbling) What the devil is she so angry about? She’s on fire about something, and Lidio doesn’t seem to have quenched it.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: O false spirits and stupid human beings! How I have been deceived! How unhappy I am! I have harmed not only myself but also him whom I love even more than myself. Miserable me, who have what I asked for and found what I wasn’t looking for! If the spirit can’t help me, I am ready to kill myself: suicide would be better than a life of misery. Here comes Ruffo; soon I shall find out what my fate is to be. No one’s in sight, so I’ll talk to him out here. That’s better than indoors, for even walls have ears.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: What is it, my lady?

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: There tears, even more than words, show you how I feel.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: But what is it? Don’t cry, my lady.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Ah, Ruffo, I don’t know if it’s my ignorance or your treachery that’s to blame.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: What are you saying, my lady?

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Whether it was my fault, or whether the heavens willed it, or whether the spirit acted maliciously –I don’t know the reason, but Lidio has been changed from a man into a woman. I discovered this when I was feeling him over. And though I have been deprived of my pleasure, I do not weep for my own sake so much as for Lidio, who because of me has lost that which he prizes most. Now you know the reason for these tears and will be able to understand what I want you to do.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: My lady, if I did not see these tears, which would be hard indeed to feign, I would have trouble believing you; but seeing that they are real, I can assure you that you need weep only for yourself. I remember you asked that Lidio visit you in the form of a woman, and now it occurs to me that the spirit, wishing to follow your instructions to the letter, sent your lover to you as a woman both in dress and in body. So cheer up, because he who could change him into a woman can change him back again into a man.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: This explanation makes me feel better already. If you can return Lidio to me whole, you shall have money, clothing, anything that is mine to give.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: I know the spirit will do as you wish, so I can promise you that he will change your lover back into a man immediately. However, in order to avoid making another mistake, state your wishes clearly this time.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: First, that he be given back the dagger for my sheath. Do you know what I mean?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Quite.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: And that he visit me in the dress of a woman, not in the body of one.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: If you had said this earlier, this mistake would not have happened. But I’m glad it did, because now you know how powerful my spirit is.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Ruffo, I beg you to relieve my suspense. I won’t have a moment’s peace of mind until I see him.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: You will be able to touch him as well as see him.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: When? Today?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: It’s late now. He’d only be able to stay with you a short time.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: He wouldn’t have to say. I would just want to make sure he was changed back into a man again.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Ah, my lady, that would be like a thirsty man going to a fountain and being unable to drink.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: He’ll come tonight, then?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: If you wish. You can wait for him just inside the door.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: That’s not necessary. As long as he’s dressed like a woman, no one will know he’s not one.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: As you wish.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Be of good cheer, Ruffo. You’ll never want for anything again.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: No more will you, my lady.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: And he’ll come right away?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: The moment I get home.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: I’ll send Samia along so you can let me know what the spirit says.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Do so, and don’t forget that the lover, too, must have his reward.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Don’t worry; he’ll have money and jewels aplenty.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Go in peace. (Exit Fulvia) Love is painted blind with good reason, for he who loves never sees the truth. This woman is so blinded by her passion that she believes a spirit can make a person male or female at will, as if all that had to be done to make a woman out of a man was to pull out the root and replace it with a crack, and then, to turn him back into a man, sew up the mouth down there and replace it with a peg. Oh, the credulity of lovers! Ah, here comes Lidio and Fannio; I see they have already changed their clothes.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: You must get dressed up again.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: To go back to Fulvia. Ha, ha!

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Why are you giggling in that obscene way?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Come, what is it?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Ha, ha! Fulvia, believing the spirit changed Lidio into a woman, wants him to change back into a man again and revisit her.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: What did you tell her?

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: That it would be done right away.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: You said the right thing.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: When will you go back then?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I don’t know.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: You don’t seem very enthusiastic. Don’t you want to?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Yes, we’ll go.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: You must be sure to do so, because I told her the spirit promised you would.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Don’t worry. We’ll go back.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: When?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Just as soon as we finish our errand, we’ll dress up again and go back.

sp.speaker: Ruffo
sp.p: Don’t fail to do so. I see her maid standing in the door; I don’t want her to see me talking with you, so good-bye. Oh, wait! Fannio, let me have a word with you privately. This time, see that our dainty gentleman uses his pestle instead of his mortar with the lady Fulvia.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: I’ll do that. Good-bye.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Samia is coming out. Let’s step aside and let her go by without seeing us.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: She is talking to herself.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Be quiet, and listen.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: This is what comes of meddling with the spirits: just see what they’ve done to Lidio.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: She’s talking about you.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: First they made a woman out of him, and now they want to make a man out of him; this is a hard day for him and for me, too. But if they succeed, everything will be all right. I’ll soon find out, because my mistress has sent me to ask the magician. She is so sure of the outcome that she is getting together a sum of money to give to Lidio.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Did you hear that about the money?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I did.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Then let’s get ready to go back.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Fannie, you must be out of your mind. I don’t know what you could have been thinking about to promise Ruffo that we’d go back there.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Why can’t we?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Silly man, as if you didn’t know I am a woman.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: So what?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: So what, he says! Don’t you know, stupid, that if I reveal my sex, I’ll bring harm to myself, disappointment to Fulvia, and cause Ruffo to lose his standing with her? How can you prevent that?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: You ask how?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Where there are men, there are means.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: But where there are only women, like her and me, the means are lacking.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Don’t worry. When I promised Ruffo that you would revisit the lady Fulvia, I knew what I was doing: I had it all figured out.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Didn’t you tell me it was dark in her bedroom?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Yes, it was.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: And that she did not talk with you but only felt you with her hands?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: That’s right.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Well, I’ll go there with you, they way we did before.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Yes?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: That is. I’ll go as a maid.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Well, and then?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Dressed as a woman, like yourself.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I understand that. But then what?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: When you get in her room, pretend you have something to say to me. Come out of the room and take my place outside while I go inside and pretend to be you. She won’t be able to tell the difference in the darkness. She’ll think the spirit has changed you back into a man: we shall have all the money we want, and moreover I’ll be able to enjoy myself.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Fannio, I never heard of a cleverer plan than this.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: So you see I was right to tell Ruffo we would go back.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Indeed you were. But in the meantime it would be a good idea to find out what’s going on at the house about this wedding of mine.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: As to that, I see no way out: better not think about it in advance.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Putting things off is not going to solve them. They won’t look any better tomorrow than they do today.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Who can say? One thing at a time. Where the lady Fulvia is concerned we stand only to gain.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: All right, but first go to my house and find out from Tiresia what is going on. Come back quickly, and then we’ll go to Fulvia’s.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: I will.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What seems to be the trouble?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: My mistress has the devil in her.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Ah?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: The magician changed Lidio into a woman.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: You think it’s funny?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Indeed I do.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: It’s the gospel truth.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: You’re not serious, are you?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Of course I am, stupid. And whether you believe it or not, that’s what’s happened. My mistress felt of him and found out he was a woman.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Well, what’s she going to do now?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: You don’t believe me, so I’m not going to tell you.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I swear I do. Tell me what she’s going to do next.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: The spirit is going to change him back into a man. I have just been to see Ruffo; he was given me this note to take to my mistress.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Let me read it.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Oh, no! Something might happen to you.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Even if I should drop dead, I want to see it.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Fessenio, be careful. Don’t meddle with the spirits.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I’m not afraid. Show it to me.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Don’t, Fessenio. Or at least cross yourself first.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Come, let’s have a look.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Well, all right... but you must promise to be as silent as the grave. If anyone found out I let you see it, it would be bad for both of us.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Don’t worry. Give it here.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Read it out loud.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: (reading) Greetings from Ruffo to Fulvia. The spirit, when he learned the effect of what he had done, was much amused. No one was to blame but yourself, but rest assured that he will restore to your lover the part that is now missing and send him back to you right away. He says moreover that Lidio loves you more than ever, so much so that he will never again give his heart to anyone else. But that you are not to speak to anyone of this, or a dreadful scandal might result. That, finally, you are to send money to him and also to the spirit, to show your gratitude both to him and to me. Be of good cheer, and do not forget your faithful servant Ruffo.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Now you see it is true there is nothing the spirits do not know and cannot do.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I can hardy believe it.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: I am anxious to bring this good news to my mistress.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Go, and God be with you. (Exit Samia.) Good heavens, am I to believe that Lidio has really been changed into a man by magic, and that he will never love anyone again except Fulvia? Only God could work such a miracle, and yet Samia says that Fulvia felt him carefully. I intend to see this miracle with my own eyes, before he changes into a man again, and then, if it’s as she says, I’ll worship this magician forever. I’ll go to Lidio now; I may find him at home.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: How true it is that women do to money what the sun does to ice: they consume it completely. My mistress no sooner read Ruffo's note than she gave me this bag of money to take to Lidio. There he is now. Now, Lidio, you will see how the lady Fulvia keeps her word. (To Santilla.) Come, here it is. Take it.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Here I am.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: No, give it here.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Oh, I made a mistake. (To Santilla.) Excuse me, sir. I wanted this gentleman, not you.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Now you are mistaken. Come, do your business with me, and let that gentleman go.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: You are right; I’m sorry. (To Lidio.) Good-bye, sir. (To Santilla.) You come here.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: What do you mean good-bye? Here, look at me.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: (To Lidio) Oh, yes... it is you after all. (To Santilla.) It’s this gentleman I want. You may leave us.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Leave you? What do you mean? Am I not Lidio?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Why, yes, I think you are. (To Lidio.) You go away, sir.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: What’s the matter with you? Look at me carefully. Am I not the one?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Why, of course. I’m sorry. You are Lidio. (To Santilla.) You leave us, please.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: You fool, I am Lidio; he’s not.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Well, well, you are right. (To Lidio.) Do please leave us alone.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: What are you trying to do, you bitch? You know the money belongs to me, yet you want to give it to this fellow.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: What do you mean, yours? Give it to me.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: No, to me.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Why to you? You are not Lidio; I am.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Give it here.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Here!

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Don’t touch it, either of you, or I’ll scream. Let me have a good look at you both. Good, God, what a miracle! These two resemble each other more than snow resembles snow, or one egg another. I don’t know which of you is Lidio: first it seems the one, then the other. But I know how I’ll find out. Tell me, is either of you gentlemen in love?

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: I am.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: And so am I.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Which one?

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: I.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Where does this money come from?

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: From a lady.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: From my sweetheart.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Oh, heavens! Still not clear. Tell me, who is this sweetheart?

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Fulvia.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Fulvia.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Which of you is her lover?

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: I am.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I am.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: What do you mean, you are?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I mean I am.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: You’re not. I am.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Ah, me, what is all this? Which Fulvia are you talking about?

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Calandro’s wife.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: (To Samia) And your mistress.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Still no light. Either I have lost my mind, or these men are bewitched. Tell me, how were you dressed when you went to her?

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: As a woman.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: As a young lady.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: This is too much. But oh, now I will find out. When did my mistress want her lover to visit her?

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: By day.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: At midday.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: What the devil! This is certainly a fiendish plot of some kind, thought up by that damned spirit. I’d better go back to my mistress with this money and let her give it to whomever she wishes. Gentlemen, I’m sure you understand –I don’t know which of you to give it to. My mistress will surely know who her lover is, so whichever of you is Lidio go to see her and you may be sure that she will give it to you.

p.seg: My own reflection in the mirror looks less like me than does this fellow; I shall soon know who he is. Such adventures don’t happen every day, and Fulvia may change her mind. This is quite a lot of money. I’d better go pay her a visit, the way I used to.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: That must be the man that I was mistaken for. I wonder what is keeping Fannio? If he were here, as he said he would be, we could go to Fulvia’s and maybe collect a lot of money. But he’s not, and I have to do something about this wedding I’m supposed to be in.

p.seg: I couldn’t find Lidio anywhere.
What am I going to do now?

If I don’t get to the bottom of this, and find out if it’s true that Lidio has been changed into a woman, it won’t be my fault. Oh! Is that him over there? No, I don’t think so. Yes, it is. He does seem changed.
Ah, me!
He is talking to himself.
What a mess all this is!
I wonder what’s the matter?
Must I be ruined so soon?
What ruin is he talking about?
Because of too much love?
I wonder what he means by that.
Will I have to stop wearing these clothes?
My, my, his voice certainly has become feminine. What a pity!
And lose all the freedom I have enjoyed?
Well, it’s true, all right. There’s no longer any doubt about it.
Now everyone will know I’m a woman. I’ll never be able to pass for a man again.
True enough. The harm’s been done now.
From now on I must call myself Santilla, and not Lidio.
Sad but true.
I’d be better off if they had let me die the day Modone was captured.
Oh, cruel fate! He’s taking this very hard. If I hadn’t heard it from his own lips, I’d never believe it. I’ll speak to him.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Who is this wretch?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why do you call me a wretch, as if you didn’t know who I am?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I never knew you and I don’t care to.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: So you don’t know your own servant anymore?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: You my servant?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: If you don’t want me, I’ll be someone else’s.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Please leave me alone. I have no time for drunkards.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Either you are drunk or you have lost your memory. But don’t think you can hide from me, because I know all about your little accident.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: What accident?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: When the magician changed you into a woman.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I a woman?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Yes, a woman.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: You are mistaken. (Fessenio approaches, attempts to feel her.) You wretch! What are you trying to do?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: I want to make sure.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: How dare you touch me, you brute?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: (persisting) I’ll find out or die in the attempt.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Miserable creature, don’t you dare! Help! Fannio! Help!

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: What’s going on here?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: This impudent fellow claims that I am a woman, and is trying to feel me against my will.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: How dare you do such a thing?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What right have you to come between my master and me?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Your master?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Of course. Why?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: My good man, you are mistaken. I know for a fact that you are not his servant, nor he your master, because I am his servant, and he is my master.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: That cannot be. I am his servant, and he is my master. You are both lying.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I’m not surprised that you speak with such arrogance, since you acted with such presumption.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Nor am I surprised that you have forgotten who I am, since you have forgotten your own identity.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: (to Fessenio) Mind what you say to him.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I don’t know my own identity?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: My lord, or rather my lady, if you knew who you were, you would know who I am.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I know well enough who I am, but as for you, I have no idea.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Say rather that in losing yourself you have found someone else.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: And who is it that I have found?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Your sister Santilla, for now, since you have changed into a woman, she is in you; and since you are no longer a man, you have lost yourself. You are no longer Lidio.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Lidio? Who is Lidio?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Poor fellow! He doesn’t remember a thing. Come, master, don’t you remember being Lidio of Medone, son of Demetrius, brother of Santilla, pupil of Polinico, master of Fessenio, lover of the lady Fulvia?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Fannio, did you hear that? Oh, yes, I know the lady Fulvia.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: He remembers no one but Fulvia; it’s obvious he’s been bewitched.

div2.head: Scene III
div2.stage: Lidio in women’s dress, Fessenio, Santilla as Lidio, Fannio

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Fessenio, oh, Fessenio!

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Who is that woman waving to me? (To Fannio.) You wait –I haven’t finished with you yet.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Fannio, if I dared to think that my brother was still alive, I would be full of hope. That person (indicating Lidio) must be the one they have mistaken me for.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: You are not sure of your brother’s death?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: By no means.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: For now I am quite certain that that is indeed our lost Lidio, and now it seems to me that I also recognize this man as – Fessenio!

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Oh, God, I begin to feel my heart grow light with joy.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: (to Lidio) I’m still not sure if you are Lidio or if the other one is. Let me have a better look at you.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: What’s the matter with you? Have you been drinking?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Yes, you are Lidio all right, and you are a man, too.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: I am on my way to see the lady Fulvia.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: That’s right; she’s waiting to give you the money.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: What’s that you said?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: If I’ve said or done anything to offend you, I beg your pardon, for now I realize that you have been mistaken for my master.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Who is your master?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: One Lidio of Modone, and he looks so much like you I thought you were he.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Dear Fannio, everything is clear now. (To Fessenio) What is your name?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Fessenio, sir, at your service.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Now there is no longer any doubt of it. Oh, how happy we are! (Embraces Fessenio.) Dear Fessenio, you are mine!

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What are all these caresses for? And why do you say I am yours? When I said I was your servant a moment ago, I was lying: I am not, not are you my master. I have another master, so you must seek another servant.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: You are mine, and I am yours!

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: (embraces Fessenio) Oh, my dear Fessenio!

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What does all this mean? Something’s going on here that I don’t know about.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: This is Santilla, your master’s sister.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Our Santilla?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Shh, no so loud. Yes, it is. And I am Fannio.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: (embraces Fannio.) Fannio! My dear fellow!

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: Not here; someone’s coming. Don’t say anything about it.

div2.head: Scene IV
div2.stage: Samia, Fessenio, Santilla as Lidio, Fannio

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Boohoo! Boohoo! My mistress and I are done for. Ruined! And out of a clear sky. Boohoo!

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What’s the matter with you, Samia?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Oh, my poor mistress!

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why, what’s the matter?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Oh, my dear Fessenio, we are done for.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: But what is it? Come, speak up.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Bad news.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: How so?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Calandro’s brothers founds your master Lidio with my mistress. They have sent for Calandro and for her brothers, too. They are going to denounce her to them and maybe kill Lidio.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: What’s this? Oh, my poor master! Are they holding him prisoner?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Why didn’t he run away then?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Because of my mistress. She is in hopes that before Calandro and her brothers get to the house, the magician will change Lidio back into a woman. That way he’ll keep his life and my mistress her reputation: if he saved himself now, by running away, she would surely be ruined. That’s where I’m going now –to see Ruffo.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Wait a minute. What part of the house is Lidio in?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Both he and my mistress are in the bedroom on the first floor.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Isn’t there a window in the rear of that room?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Yes, he could escape easily enough if he wanted to.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: That’s not why I asked. If someone were to slip in through that window, would he be notice?

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Probably not.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Samia, this magician business is a lot of nonsense. If you want to save you mistress, go back to the house, and if there’s anybody in the hall, try to get rid of them.

sp.speaker: Samia
sp.p: Well, all right. I’ll do as you say, but I hope you know what you’re doing.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Don’t worry. Run along now.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Ah, me, Fessenio, it look as if fate has arranged that I should no sooner find my brother than I should lose him again; no sooner does he come to life than he must lose it.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Now is no time for tears: this situation calls for quick action and clear thinking. No one is looking now, so swap clothes with Fannio. Quickly –that’s it. Don’t worry; I’m coming with you. Fannio, you wait here. Now, Santilla, I’ll tell you what you must do.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: What a strange predicament this brother and sister find themselves in! This will either be the happiest or the worst day of their lives, depending on how it ends. It seems that heaven made them similar not only in their appearance but also in their fortunes: each of them is now in a position where what profits one profits both and where what harms one harms the other. Until I can see further ahead I am unable either to rejoice or despair, fear or hope. I pray heaven that Lidio and Santilla will somehow find a way out of all this. In the meantime, I’ll step aside and wait for the outcome.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: I have been delivered from great danger, and I scarcely know how it happened. While I was in that room, bewailing the misfortune that overtook my mistress and me, someone sent by Fessenio jumps into the room through the rear window, dressed himself in my clothes, and gives me his. Then Fessenio told me to slip out the window, saying not to worry, that everything would turn out all right. Just a few moments ago things couldn’t have looked worse; now I am pleased with the way they seem to be working out. Fessenio stayed behind to tell Fulvia something. I’d better wait here to see what happens. Oh, there is my mistress now, standing on the threshold. She looks happy, too.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: This has been quite a day for me, but everything has turned out for the best, thank heaven. I couldn’t be more pleased: my reputation has been saved and so has Lidio’s life. And now it will be easier than ever for me to see him as often as I like. Whoever wouldn’t be satisfied with that wouldn’t be human.

div2.head: Scene VII
div2.stage: Calandro, accompanied by two of Fulvia’s brothers, Fulvia

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Wretched woman, what are you doing at that door? How can you stand there and wait for me like that, knowing you have hung horns on me? I don’t know how I can keep myself from beating the breath out of your body, but first I want you to see me kill the man you have in that room, you slut, and then I’m going to tear the eyes out of your head.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Alas, my husband, what is the meaning of all this? Why do you act as if I were guilty of something, when I am not? What is the reason for such cruelty?

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: Shameless woman, how can you keep pretending, as if we didn’t know you have a man in there, dressed in woman’s clothes?

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: My brothers, this wretched man wants to expose what I have always kept hidden, and that is my patience and the many outrages I have suffered at his hands. There is no wife in all the world more faithful than I, nor treated worse. And he dares to say that I have made him wear horns!

sp.speaker: Calandro
sp.p: It’s true, you miserable creature, and now I’m going to prove it to your brothers.

sp.speaker: Fulvia
sp.p: Go on in, all of you, and see who it is I have in my room that this miserable little worm says he is going to kill.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Fessenio said everything would be all right, but it doesn’t look that way, and I’m beginning to be suspicious. I didn’t know who that was he made me swap clothes with. I don’t see Fessenio, and Calandro has gone in the house, threatening Fulvia. He is beside himself with rage and may hurt her. If I hear any trouble, I’ll go inside, no matter what, and either protect her or die for her. No true lover was ever lacking in courage.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: There is Lidio over there, or rather Santilla. Let’s change again. Give me back my clothes, and I’ll give you yours.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Why, what do you mean?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: It’s been such a short time since Fessenio made you change clothes that you can’t have forgotten. Come, give me those and take these.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Certainly I remember changing clothes, but those aren’t the ones I gave you.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: What’s wrong with you? Do you think I’d have gone and sold them?

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Don’t make me angry. Oh, there is Fessenio.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! They thought that under that dress they’d find the young man they suspected Fulvia of amusing herself with: they were going to kill him and denounce her, but when they found out it was a girl, they quieted down and apologized to Fulvia, saying she was the most virtuous woman in all the world. Now her reputation is secure, and so is my own happiness. They have let Santilla go; I see her coming out now. And there is Lidio, too.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Where is my brother, Fessenio?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: There he is over there, still wearing the clothes you gave him. Let’s go to him. Lidio, do you know who this is?

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Not for sure. Tell me.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: The one who saved you by taking your place at the lady Fulvia’s, and for whom you have been looking so long.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Who?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Your Santilla.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: My sister?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I am you sister, and you are my brother.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Are you really Santilla? But I see now that you are. Oh, my dear sister, for whom I have wished and searched so long! Now at last I am satisfied; now I have gained my wish; now I am the happiest man alive.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Beloved brother of mine, though I see you and touch you, I can scarcely believe you are really he whom I thought dead and for whom I mourned so long. Now that I find you are alive, my joy is as great as my grief was then.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: And I, my dear sister, love you all the more because of what you did for me today: if it hadn’t been for you, I wouldn’t be alive to say this.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Now that I have recovered somewhat from this shock, allow me to present to you our servant Fannio, who has always served me faithfully.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Dear Fannio, I remember you quite well, and in having served one of us you have served us both. You shall be rewarded for it.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: My greatest reward, sir, is to see you alive and rejoined with your sister.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Dear Fessenio, why are you looking at us so hard?

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: Never in all my life have I seen a man resemble another man so much as you and your brother resemble each other. I understand now the reason for all these strange mistakes.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: They have been strange indeed.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: And more numerous than either of you realizes.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: We’ll have time to talk about that later. Right now the most important thing is this: when I told the lady Fulvia that this was your sister Santilla, she was greatly pleased and said that, if everyone is willing, Santilla would become the wife of her son Flaminio.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: Now I understand why, when we were in the room together, she kissed me tenderly and said: I don’t know which of us three is the happiest; Lidio has found a sister, I a daughter, and you a husband.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: It could all be true, too.

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: I know of a better plan still.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: What is that?

sp.speaker: Fannio
sp.p: As Fessenio says, you two are so much alike that you would fool anybody.

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: I know what you mean –that Lidio should take my place in the marriage with Perillo’s daughter.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: That’s settled then?

sp.speaker: Santilla
sp.p: As settled as the weather.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: How fortunate we are! After so fierce a storm, how beautiful a calm! We shall be even better off than we were in Modone.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: As much better off than Italy is worthier than Greece; than Rome is statelier tha Modone; and than two fortunes are better than one. We shall all be gainers.

sp.speaker: Lidio
sp.p: Come, let’s get started.

sp.speaker: Fessenio
sp.p: (to audience) Good people, the weddings will take place tomorrow. Whoever wishes to see them should stay, but whoever to avoid the inconvenience of waiting till then, let him go about his business, as we are finished with ours. VALETE ET PLAUDITE.
